sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.text: 3 Methodology Analogous to the cognitive mechanisms of human memory, we design the ES-Mem framework as illustrated in Figure 2 . It comprises two core components: a Dynamic Event Segmentation model and a Hierarchical Memory Architecture . Specifically, the latter is composed of Layered Memory Construction and a Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval strategy. 3.1 Dynamic Event Segmentation We define a dialogue event as a temporal segment centered on a stable topic or intent, characterized by high internal semantic homogeneity and bounded by distinct shifts in topic, task phases, or interaction patterns. To effectively capture these boundaries, we propose a two-stage segmentation strategy that integrates topic coherence detection with intent-aware boundary refinement. Stage 1: Topic Coherence Detection. Given a dialogue session [LaTeX: \mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{T}\}] 𝒰 = { u 1 , u 2 , … , u T } \mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{T}\} consisting of [LaTeX: T] T T turns, we first employ an LLM to extract a concise topic representation for each turn [LaTeX: u_{t}] u t u_{t} . To mitigate semantic drift and ensure temporal continuity, we adopt a recurrent extraction scheme: the LLM is conditioned on the concatenation of the previous turn’s topic output and the current turn’s content. This generates a smoothed topic evolution trajectory [LaTeX: h_{t}] h t h_{t} . We then utilize an embedding model to map these textual topics into a sequence of normalized vectors [LaTeX: \mathbf{H}=\{\mathbf{h}_{1},\mathbf{h}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{T}\}] 𝐇 = { 𝐡 1 , 𝐡 2 , … , 𝐡 T } \mathbf{H}=\{\mathbf{h}_{1},\mathbf{h}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{T}\} . To quantify the semantic coupling between adjacent turns, we assume the dimensions of the topic vectors [LaTeX: \mathbf{h}_{t}] 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} and [LaTeX: \mathbf{h}_{t+1}] 𝐡 t + 1 \mathbf{h}_{t+1} follow a joint Gaussian distribution. Let random variables [LaTeX: X=\mathbf{h}_{t}] X = 𝐡 t X=\mathbf{h}_{t} and [LaTeX: Y=\mathbf{h}_{t+1}] Y = 𝐡 t + 1 Y=\mathbf{h}_{t+1} . We compute the Pearson correlation coefficient [LaTeX: \rho_{t}] ρ t \rho_{t} across their dimensions: [LaTeX: \rho_{t}=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)}}] ρ t = Cov ⁡ ( X , Y ) Var ⁡ ( X ) ​ Var ​ ( Y ) \rho_{t}=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)\mathrm{Var}(Y)}} (1) Under the Gaussian assumption, the Mutual Information (MI) between [LaTeX: X] X X and [LaTeX: Y] Y Y can be derived as: [LaTeX: I_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\bigl(1-\rho_{t}^{2}\bigr)] I t = − 1 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 − ρ t 2 ) I_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\bigl(1-\rho_{t}^{2}\bigr) (2) Here, [LaTeX: I_{t}] I t I_{t} serves as a proxy for topical consistency. A sharp decline in [LaTeX: I_{t}] I t I_{t} indicates a rupture in semantic coupling, signaling a potential event boundary. We compute the global MI sequence for the session and identify a set of candidate boundaries [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} by selecting time steps where [LaTeX: I_{t}] I t I_{t} falls below a dynamic quantile threshold [LaTeX: q] q q (e.g., the bottom 35%): [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}=\{t\mid I_{t}\leq\mathrm{Quantile}_{q}(\mathbf{I})\}] 𝒞 = { t ∣ I t ≤ Quantile q ​ ( 𝐈 ) } \mathcal{C}=\{t\mid I_{t}\leq\mathrm{Quantile}_{q}(\mathbf{I})\} . Stage 2: Intent-Aware Boundary Refinement. The candidate set [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} derived from statistical metrics may contain noise. Therefore, we introduce a second stage of intent-level verification using an LLM to align the segmentation with cognitive event theory. For each candidate boundary [LaTeX: t\in\mathcal{C}] t ∈ 𝒞 t\in\mathcal{C} , we construct local context windows comprising the preceding and succeeding [LaTeX: L] L L turns: [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{t}=\{u_{t-L+1},\ldots,u_{t}\}] ℒ t = { u t − L + 1 , … , u t } \mathcal{L}_{t}=\{u_{t-L+1},\ldots,u_{t}\} and [LaTeX: \mathcal{R}_{t}=\{u_{t+1},\ldots,u_{t+L}\}] ℛ t = { u t + 1 , … , u t + L } \mathcal{R}_{t}=\{u_{t+1},\ldots,u_{t+L}\} . This localized context enables the LLM to discern subtle shifts in intent without ingesting the entire history. Drawing inspiration from Lee et al. (2025) , we define a label set partitioned into boundary-positive labels [LaTeX: \mathcal{Y}_{\text{shift}}] 𝒴 shift \mathcal{Y}_{\text{shift}} (e.g., Topic_Shift , Topic_Intro ) and boundary-negative labels [LaTeX: \mathcal{Y}_{\text{cont}}] 𝒴 cont \mathcal{Y}_{\text{cont}} (e.g., Detail_Elaborate , Direct_Resp ). The taxonomy is detailed in Appendix Figure 7 . The LLM analyzes the transition from [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{t}] ℒ t \mathcal{L}_{t} to [LaTeX: \mathcal{R}_{t}] ℛ t \mathcal{R}_{t} and outputs the most probable labels along with their confidence scores [LaTeX: c_{t}\in[0,1]] c t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{t}\in[0,1] . We formulate the probability of [LaTeX: t] t t being a valid event boundary, [LaTeX: p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t)] p eb ​ ( t ) p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t) , by aggregating the model’s confidence in shift versus continuation: [LaTeX: p(y_{t})=\begin{cases}c_{t},&\text{if }y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{shift}}\\ 1-c_{t},&\text{if }y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{cont}}\end{cases}] p ⁡ ( y t ) = { c t , if ​ y t ∈ 𝒴 shift 1 − c t , if ​ y t ∈ 𝒴 cont p(y_{t})=\begin{cases}c_{t},&\text{if }y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{shift}}\\ 1-c_{t},&\text{if }y_{t}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\text{cont}}\end{cases} (3) To ensure robustness, we average the probabilities derived from the highest confidence prediction ( [LaTeX: p_{h}] p h p_{h} ) and the lowest confidence prediction ( [LaTeX: p_{l}] p l p_{l} ): [LaTeX: p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(p(y_{t}^{\text{high}})+p(y_{t}^{\text{low}})\bigr)] p eb ​ ( t ) = 1 2 ​ ( p ⁡ ( y t high ) + p ⁡ ( y t low ) ) p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(p(y_{t}^{\text{high}})+p(y_{t}^{\text{low}})\bigr) (4) Finally, we apply a confidence threshold [LaTeX: \tau_{c}] τ c \tau_{c} . Positions satisfying [LaTeX: p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t)\geq\tau_{c}] p eb ​ ( t ) ≥ τ c p_{\mathrm{eb}}(t)\geq\tau_{c} constitute the final boundary set [LaTeX: \mathcal{B}] ℬ \mathcal{B} , partitioning the dialogue into semantically coherent and structurally distinct event units. 3.2 Layered Memory Construction Unlike previous approaches that rely on flat storage or complex graph structures, we construct a layered memory comprising three levels: Level 1: Refined Boundaries , Level 2: Event Summaries , and Level 3: Raw Context . After dynamic event segmentation, the memory repository is defined as [LaTeX: \mathcal{M}=\{M_{1},M_{2},\ldots,M_{n}\}] ℳ = { M 1 , M 2 , … , M n } \mathcal{M}=\{M_{1},M_{2},\ldots,M_{n}\} . Each memory unit [LaTeX: M_{i}] M i M_{i} is formally represented as: [LaTeX: M_{i}=(b_{i}^{\text{ref}},s_{i},r_{i},t_{i}),\quad\forall M_{i}\in\mathcal{M}] M i = ( b i ref , s i , r i , t i ) , ∀ M i ∈ ℳ M_{i}=(b_{i}^{\text{ref}},s_{i},r_{i},t_{i}),\quad\forall M_{i}\in\mathcal{M} (5) where [LaTeX: t_{i}] t i t_{i} denotes the timestamp of the event. Level 1: Refined Event Boundaries ( [LaTeX: b_{i}^{\text{ref}}] b i ref b_{i}^{\text{ref}} ). Existing memory mechanisms predominantly focus on the internal semantic content of individual events, typically neglecting the explicit modeling of boundaries or state transitions. This oversight results in a loss of critical structural cues that serve as natural cognitive anchors for retrieval. To address this gap, we propose a Refined Boundary Representation that explicitly models the state transition between events. Specifically, we employ an LLM to generate a textual description of the transition from event [LaTeX: M_{i-1}] M i − 1 M_{i-1} to [LaTeX: M_{i}] M i M_{i} , leveraging their summaries ( [LaTeX: s_{i-1},s_{i}] s i − 1 , s i s_{i-1},s_{i} ) and the raw boundary context ( [LaTeX: c_{i}^{\text{raw}}] c i raw c_{i}^{\text{raw}} , consisting of the last [LaTeX: L] L L turns of [LaTeX: M_{i-1}] M i − 1 M_{i-1} and the first [LaTeX: L] L L turns of [LaTeX: M_{i}] M i M_{i} ). The generation process is formalized as: [LaTeX: b_{i}^{\text{ref}}=\text{LLM}_{\text{gen}}(s_{i-1},s_{i},c_{i}^{\text{raw}})] b i ref = LLM gen ​ ( s i − 1 , s i , c i raw ) b_{i}^{\text{ref}}=\text{LLM}_{\text{gen}}(s_{i-1},s_{i},c_{i}^{\text{raw}}) (6) The resulting [LaTeX: b_{i}^{\text{ref}}] b i ref b_{i}^{\text{ref}} follows a structured format (e.g., “ Topic A ended. Transitioned to Topic B. Context: … ”), serving as a high-level cognitive anchor. Level 2: Event Summaries ( [LaTeX: s_{i}] s i s_{i} ). Generated during the dynamic event segmentation phase, the event summary [LaTeX: s_{i}] s i s_{i} is composed of the core topics and keywords extracted from each dialogue turn within the event. This dense semantic representation serves as the index for fine-grained content matching, bridging the gap between high-level conceptual anchors and low-level verbatim details. Level 3: Raw Context ( [LaTeX: r_{i}] r i r_{i} ). This level stores the verbatim dialogue records, preserving the complete temporal sequence and semantic fidelity of the original interaction. While Level 1 and Level 2 are used for efficient indexing and retrieval, [LaTeX: r_{i}] r i r_{i} serves as the ground truth source provided to the dialogue agent for final response generation, ensuring that the generated answers are factually accurate and contextually consistent. 3.3 Coarse-to-Fine Retrieval Prevalent flat retrieval paradigms often struggle to locate specific episodic contexts within massive historical data due to the lack of structural guidance. To mitigate this, we propose a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that mimics the human cognitive process of “scanning anchors [LaTeX: \to] → \to unpacking details.” This process consists of three stages. Stage 1: Boundary Scanning (Anchor Retrieval). Given a query [LaTeX: q] q q , we first encode it into vector [LaTeX: e_{q}] e q e_{q} . Instead of matching the query against all event details immediately, we explicitly calculate the similarity between the query and the Refined Boundaries (Level 1) to identify potential state transitions or topic shifts relevant to the query: [LaTeX: \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(q,i)=\cos(e_{q},e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}})=\frac{e_{q}\cdot e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}}}{\lVert e_{q}\rVert\lVert e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}}\rVert}] sim bnd ​ ( q , i ) = cos ⁡ ( e q , e i bnd ) = e q ⋅ e i bnd ∥ e q ∥ ​ ∥ e i bnd ∥ \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(q,i)=\cos(e_{q},e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}})=\frac{e_{q}\cdot e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}}}{\lVert e_{q}\rVert\lVert e_{i}^{\mathrm{bnd}}\rVert} (7) We select the top- [LaTeX: k] k k events with the highest boundary similarity scores to form the anchor set [LaTeX: \mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}\}] 𝒜 = { a 1 , a 2 , … , a k } \mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}\} . These anchors represent the moments where the conversation context aligns most closely with the user’s inquiry intent. Stage 2: Activated Memory Interval Expansion. Relying solely on single time-point boundaries may miss the full context of an evolving discussion. Therefore, we treat each anchor [LaTeX: a\in\mathcal{A}] a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} as a center point and expand a temporal window of size [LaTeX: w] w w to define an Activated Memory Interval . The candidate set [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is formed by the union of these intervals: [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}=\bigcup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\{j\mid|j-a|\leq w\}] 𝒞 = ⋃ a ∈ 𝒜 { j ∣ | j − a | ≤ w } \mathcal{C}=\bigcup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\{j\mid|j-a|\leq w\} (8) This step significantly filters the search space, focusing only on logically relevant intervals. Importantly, each candidate event [LaTeX: j\in\mathcal{C}] j ∈ 𝒞 j\in\mathcal{C} inherits a context score [LaTeX: S_{\text{ctx}}(j)] S ctx ​ ( j ) S_{\text{ctx}}(j) from its generating anchor, defined as the maximum boundary score within its influential window: [LaTeX: S_{\text{ctx}}(j)=\max_{\{a\in\mathcal{A}\mid j\in\text{window}(a)\}}\mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(q,a)] S ctx ​ ( j ) = max { a ∈ 𝒜 ∣ j ∈ window ​ ( a ) } ⁡ sim bnd ​ ( q , a ) S_{\text{ctx}}(j)=\max_{\{a\in\mathcal{A}\mid j\in\text{window}(a)\}}\mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{bnd}}(q,a) (9) Stage 3: Summary Reranking and Fusion. In the final stage, we perform fine-grained matching within the candidate set [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} using Level 2 Event Summaries. We compute the content similarity [LaTeX: \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{sum}}(q,j)] sim sum ​ ( q , j ) \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{sum}}(q,j) for each [LaTeX: j\in\mathcal{C}] j ∈ 𝒞 j\in\mathcal{C} . The final ranking score is a fusion of the specific content match and the inherited context relevance: [LaTeX: Score(j)=\alpha S_{\text{sum}}(j)+(1-\alpha)S_{\text{ctx}}(j)] S ​ c ​ o ​ r ​ e ​ ( j ) = α ​ S sum ​ ( j ) + ( 1 − α ) ​ S ctx ​ ( j ) Score(j)=\alpha S_{\text{sum}}(j)+(1-\alpha)S_{\text{ctx}}(j) (10) where [LaTeX: \alpha] α \alpha is a balancing hyperparameter and [LaTeX: S_{\text{sum}}(j)] S sum ​ ( j ) S_{\text{sum}}(j) denotes [LaTeX: \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{sum}}(q,j)] sim sum ​ ( q , j ) \mathrm{sim}_{\mathrm{sum}}(q,j) . We select the top- [LaTeX: K] K K events with the highest final scores and retrieve their raw records [LaTeX: r_{j}] r j r_{j} (Level 3) to construct the context for the LLM agent response.

title: ES-Mem: Event Segmentation-Based Memory for Long-Term Dialogue Agents
